course.description: Learn Python from scratch: setup, data types, functions, OOP, files and error handling, then finish by building a quiz game and an automation script.

lessons.title: Python Setup & First Program
lessons.body:
Python Setup & First Program

Python is a beginner-friendly programming language used for web apps, data analysis, automation and AI. To start, install Python 3 from python.org, then check it works by opening a terminal and typing python --version. You should see something like Python 3.12.0.

Write code in any text editor or in VS Code. Save your first file as hello.py and run it with python hello.py. The print() function displays text on the screen, and input() asks the user to type something. Anything after a # is a comment and is ignored by Python.

print("Hello, World!")
name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello, " + name + "! Welcome to Python.")

Step by step: print("Hello, World!") shows a greeting. input() waits for the user to type a name and stores it as text in name. The last line joins three pieces of text with + and prints a personal greeting.

Key points

  • Check Python is installed with python --version.
  • Python files end in .py and run with python filename.py.
  • print() displays output and input() reads text from the user.
  • input() always returns a string, even when the user types digits.
  • Use # for comments that explain your code.

flowchart.title: From writing code to seeing output

video.title: Learn Python - Full Course for Beginners [Tutorial]

mcqs.q: Which command checks the installed Python version?
mcqs.why: python --version asks the interpreter to print its version number.

mcqs.q: What does print("Hello") display?
mcqs.why: print() outputs the text inside the quotes without the quotes.

mcqs.q: Which line is a comment in Python?
mcqs.why: Python comments start with #; // and /* */ belong to other languages.

mcqs.q: What type of value does input() always return?
mcqs.why: input() reads keystrokes as text, so even "42" comes back as the string "42".

mcqs.q: What file extension do Python programs use?
mcqs.why: Python source files use the .py extension.

lessons.title: Data Types & Control Flow
lessons.body:
Data Types & Control Flow

Every value in Python has a type. int is a whole number like 42, float is a decimal like 3.14, str is text like "Asha", and bool is True or False. Use type() to check a value's type, and int() or str() to convert between types.

Programs make decisions with if, elif and else. A comparison such as age >= 18 produces True or False. Use == to test equality (a single = assigns a value), and combine conditions with and, or and not.

age = 20
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")
elif age >= 13:
    print("Teenager")
else:
    print("Child")

Here age >= 18 is True, so Python prints "Adult" and skips the other branches. Indentation matters: the lines under each branch must be indented by the same amount, because indentation is how Python groups a block.

Key points

  • Core types are int, float, str and bool; check with type().
  • == compares values, while = assigns a value.
  • if / elif / else runs exactly one branch, chosen top to bottom.
  • Combine conditions with and, or and not.
  • Indentation defines each block — keep it consistent.

video.title: Python for Beginners - Learn Coding with Python in 1 Hour

mcqs.q: What is the type of 3.14 in Python?
mcqs.why: Numbers with a decimal point are floats; 3 is an int.

mcqs.q: What does "5" + "3" produce?
mcqs.why: Both values are strings, so + joins them as text instead of adding numbers.

mcqs.q: Which operator tests whether two values are equal?
mcqs.why: == compares values; a single = assigns a value to a variable.

mcqs.q: What does int("42") return?
mcqs.why: int() converts the string "42" into the integer 42.

mcqs.q: In if / elif / else, how many branches run?
options: Exactly one — the first whose condition is True, or else
mcqs.why: Python checks branches top to bottom and runs only the first matching one (or else).

lessons.title: Functions & Modules
lessons.body:
Functions & Modules

A function is a named block of code you can run again and again. Define one with def, give it parameters (the inputs it accepts), and use return to send a result back. Calling a function runs its body; without return it gives back None.

Modules are files of ready-made functions you reuse with import. Python ships with a standard library: math for maths, random for random numbers, datetime for dates. You can also write your own module and import it.

import math

def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"

print(greet("Asha"))
print(math.sqrt(16))

greet("Asha") returns "Hello, Asha!" and math.sqrt(16) returns 4.0. Parameters keep functions flexible: the same greet works for any name, so you write the logic once and reuse it everywhere.

Key points

  • Define functions with def and call them by name with arguments.
  • return sends a value back; without it a function returns None.
  • import brings in a module such as math or random.
  • Parameters make one function work for many different inputs.
  • Variables created inside a function are local to that function.

nodes.label: Back in main program, print the result

mcqs.q: Which keyword defines a function in Python?
mcqs.why: Functions are defined with def, as in def greet(name):.

mcqs.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
mcqs.why: A function without return finishes and gives back the special value None.

mcqs.q: How do you use the sqrt function from the math module?
mcqs.why: import math loads the module, and math.sqrt(16) calls its square-root function.

mcqs.q: What is a parameter?
options: A value returned by a function
A named input listed in a function definition
mcqs.why: Parameters are the names in the def line; arguments are the actual values passed when calling.

mcqs.q: What happens to a variable created inside a function?
options: It is saved to a file
It is shared by all functions
It is local — it does not exist outside the function
mcqs.why: Local variables live only while the function runs and are not visible outside it.

tasks.hint: Track the value of n inside the function, then the value of result outside it.

lessons.title: Object-Oriented Programming
lessons.body:
Object-Oriented Programming

Object-oriented programming (OOP) groups data and behaviour into objects. A class is the blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. The special method __init__ runs when an object is created and sets up its attributes, and self refers to the object itself.

Methods are functions defined inside a class. Inheritance lets a new class reuse another class's attributes and methods, so you write shared behaviour once and specialise it.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def bark(self):
        return self.name + " says Woof!"

buddy = Dog("Buddy")
print(buddy.bark())

Dog("Buddy") creates an object whose name is "Buddy". Calling buddy.bark() runs the method on that object, so the output is "Buddy says Woof!". A second dog, Dog("Max"), would have its own separate name.

Key points

  • A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance built from it.
  • __init__ sets up an object's attributes when it is created.
  • self refers to the object the method is running on.
  • Methods are functions inside a class and can use the object's attributes.
  • Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class.

flowchart.title: How an object is created and used

mcqs.q: Which keyword creates a class in Python?
mcqs.why: Classes are defined with the class keyword.

mcqs.q: What does __init__ do?
options: It runs when an object is created and sets up its attributes
mcqs.why: __init__ is the constructor: Python calls it automatically on creation.

mcqs.q: What does self refer to inside a method?
options: The object the method was called on
mcqs.why: self is the first parameter of a method and points at the current instance.

mcqs.q: What does buddy = Dog("Buddy") do?
options: Creates a Dog object named Buddy
mcqs.why: Calling the class name creates a new instance of that class.

mcqs.q: What is inheritance?
options: A class reusing attributes and methods from another class
mcqs.why: Inheritance lets a child class build on a parent class instead of rewriting shared code.

tasks.answer: Dog("Buddy") sets self.name to "Buddy", and bark() prints that name plus " says Woof!".

tasks.answer: __init__ must take self as its first parameter; without it, Python passes the object into name and the assignment fails.
tasks.hint: Every method's first parameter refers to the object itself.

tasks.hint: Follow the object from creation to the print statement.

lessons.title: File Handling & Exceptions
lessons.body:
File Handling & Exceptions

Programs often need to save data. open() opens a file: mode "w" writes (and erases old content), "r" reads, and "a" appends. Always use a with block — it closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs.

Things go wrong: a file may not exist, or a conversion may fail. Wrap risky code in try and handle each problem in an except block, so the program reports the problem instead of crashing.

with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Learn Python every day\n")

try:
    with open("notes.txt", "r") as f:
        print(f.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found!")

The first block writes a line to notes.txt. The second reads it back and prints it. If the file were missing, Python would raise FileNotFoundError and the except block would print "File not found!" instead of crashing.

Key points

  • Open files with open(): "w" writes, "r" reads, "a" appends.
  • Use a with block so the file is always closed properly.
  • try / except catches errors so the program can recover gracefully.
  • Catch a specific error such as FileNotFoundError, not every error blindly.
  • read() returns the whole file content as one string.

flowchart.title: Reading a file safely with try/except

mcqs.q: Which mode opens a file for writing, erasing its old content?
mcqs.why: "w" means write and truncates the file; "r" reads and "a" appends.

mcqs.q: Why use a with block when opening a file?
options: It closes the file automatically, even on error
mcqs.why: with guarantees the file is closed when the block ends, so data is saved and resources freed.

mcqs.q: Which error is raised when you open a file that does not exist?
mcqs.why: Opening a missing file in read mode raises FileNotFoundError.

mcqs.q: What does f.read() return?
options: The whole file content as one string
mcqs.why: read() with no argument returns the entire remaining content as a single string.

mcqs.q: Where does code that handles an error go?
options: In an except block after try
mcqs.why: try holds the risky code and except holds the recovery code for a matching error.

lessons.title: Capstone: Automation Script
lessons.body:
Capstone: Automation Script

Automation means writing a script that does a boring, repetitive job for you. This capstone combines everything so far: functions organise the work, loops repeat it, file handling reads and writes data, and try / except keeps one bad file from stopping the whole job.

A good script has a main() function and the guard if __name__ == "__main__":, which runs main() only when the file is executed directly — not when it is imported by another script. The os module lets the script list and rename real files.

import os

def count_txt_files(folder):
    count = 0
    for name in os.listdir(folder):
        if name.endswith(".txt"):
            count += 1
    return count

def main():
    print("Text files:", count_txt_files("."))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Step by step: os.listdir(".") lists the current folder, the loop counts names ending in .txt, and main() prints the total. The guard at the bottom is what starts the script when you run python automate.py.

Key points

  • Automation scripts combine functions, loops, files and error handling.
  • os.listdir() lists the files in a folder.
  • if __name__ == "__main__": runs code only when the file is executed directly.
  • Keep one job per function so the script is easy to test and reuse.
  • Wrap risky file work in try / except so one failure does not stop the run.

nodes.label: main() lists files in the folder

mcqs.q: What does if __name__ == "__main__": do?
options: It runs the code only when the file is executed directly
mcqs.why: When a file is run directly, Python sets __name__ to "__main__"; when imported, it is the module name.

mcqs.q: Which function lists the files in a folder?
mcqs.why: os.listdir(folder) returns a list of the names in that folder.

mcqs.q: How do you test whether a filename ends with .txt?
mcqs.why: str.endswith() returns True when the string ends with the given suffix.

mcqs.q: Why put the counting logic in its own function?
options: So it can be reused and tested on its own
mcqs.why: One job per function keeps code organised, reusable and easy to test.

mcqs.q: What should happen if one file in an automation run is unreadable?
options: Catch the error and continue with the next file
mcqs.why: try / except around each file lets the script report the problem and keep working through the rest.

lessons.title: Lists, Dictionaries & Comprehensions
lessons.body:
Lists, Dictionaries & Comprehensions

A list holds an ordered collection: scores = [90, 85, 92]. Items are numbered from 0, so scores[0] is 90. Add items with append(), remove them with remove(), and slice a range with scores[0:2], which gives [90, 85].

A dictionary stores key-value pairs: student = {"name": "Asha", "age": 20}. Look values up by key with student["name"]. A comprehension builds a collection in one line: [x ** 2 for x in range(5)] makes [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].

scores = [90, 85, 92]
scores.append(88)
print(scores[0])
print(len(scores))

squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(5)]
print(squares)

The list starts with three scores, append(88) makes four, scores[0] prints 90, and len() prints 4. The comprehension squares 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 to give [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].

Key points

  • Lists are ordered and indexed from 0; use append() to add items.
  • Dictionaries store values under keys: student["name"].
  • len() gives the number of items in a list or dictionary.
  • Comprehensions build a new list in one readable line.
  • Slicing like scores[0:2] returns a smaller list.

flowchart.title: How a list comprehension builds a list

Add the result to the new list

mcqs.q: What is scores[0] when scores = [90, 85, 92]?
mcqs.why: Python lists are indexed from 0, so index 0 is the first item, 90.

mcqs.q: What does scores.append(88) do?
options: Adds 88 to the end of the list
mcqs.why: append() adds one item to the end of a list.

mcqs.q: How do you read the value for the key "name" in student = {"name": "Asha"}?
mcqs.why: Dictionary values are looked up with square brackets and the key.

mcqs.q: What does [x ** 2 for x in range(4)] produce?
mcqs.why: It squares 0, 1, 2 and 3, giving 0, 1, 4 and 9.

mcqs.q: What does len([10, 20, 30]) return?
mcqs.why: len() counts the items in the collection — three items here.

lessons.title: Loops & Iteration Patterns
lessons.body:
Loops & Iteration Patterns

Loops repeat work. A for loop runs once per item: for i in range(3) gives i the values 0, 1 and 2. A while loop repeats while its condition stays True, so it must change something inside the loop or it never stops.

Use break to leave a loop early and continue to skip to the next round. enumerate() gives you both the position and the value as you loop, which is handy for numbered lists.

total = 0
for i in range(1, 4):
    total += i
print(total)

for index, name in enumerate(["Asha", "Ravi"]):
    print(index, name)

The first loop adds 1, then 2, then 3, so total becomes 6. The second loop prints 0 Asha and 1 Ravi — enumerate counts from 0 by default.

Key points

  • for loops over items; range(3) gives 0, 1, 2.
  • while repeats while its condition is True — always update the condition inside.
  • break exits a loop early; continue skips to the next round.
  • enumerate() gives both the index and the value.
  • Accumulate a running total by adding inside the loop.

video.title: Learn Python - Full Course for Beginners [Tutorial]

mcqs.q: What values does range(3) produce?
mcqs.why: range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3, giving 0, 1 and 2.

mcqs.q: What does break do inside a loop?
options: Pauses the loop for one second
mcqs.why: break jumps out of the loop entirely; continue only skips the current round.

mcqs.q: What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one
mcqs.why: continue jumps back to the loop header for the next item.

mcqs.q: What happens if a while loop's condition never becomes False?
mcqs.why: while keeps going as long as its condition is True, so a condition that never changes means it never stops.

mcqs.q: What does enumerate(["Asha", "Ravi"]) give on the first round?
mcqs.why: enumerate counts from 0, so the first pair is index 0 with value "Asha".

for i in range(1, 4):

tasks.hint: Add the numbers 1, 2 and 3 together.

tasks.answer: The loop never changed count, so count < 3 stayed True forever. Adding count += 1 makes count reach 3 and the loop ends.
tasks.hint: What must change inside the loop for the condition to become False?

tasks.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints 0 to 4.
tasks.answer: range(5) produces 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which the for loop then prints one by one.
tasks.hint: Which function produces a sequence of numbers?

tasks.title: Trace the while loop

tasks.answer: Following the flowchart: start with count = 0, test count < 2 (Yes) and increment to 1, test again (Yes) and increment to 2, test a third time (No) and exit the loop, then print 2.
tasks.hint: Check the condition before every round, including the final failing check.

lessons.title: Debugging & Error Handling in Practice
lessons.body:
Debugging & Error Handling in Practice

Debugging is finding and fixing mistakes. Start by reading the traceback: the last line names the error type, and the lines above show where it happened. Common errors are NameError (a name that does not exist), TypeError (the wrong type of value) and ValueError (the right type, wrong value, like int("abc")).

When you expect a problem, handle it with try / except / else / finally: except runs when an error occurs, else runs when no error occurs, and finally always runs — it is the place to close files or release resources. Add print() calls to see what your variables actually hold, and test with small inputs first.

try:
    age = int("25")
except ValueError:
    print("Please type digits only")
else:
    print("Age is", age)
finally:
    print("Done")

int("25") succeeds, so the except block is skipped, else prints "Age is 25", and finally always prints "Done". If the text had been "abc", the except block would have run instead.

Key points

  • Read the traceback bottom-up: the last line names the error.
  • NameError means an unknown name; TypeError a wrong type; ValueError a wrong value.
  • except handles an error; else runs only when no error occurs.
  • finally always runs, even when an error occurs.
  • Use print() to inspect real variable values while debugging.

nodes.label: Find the error type and line
Fix the code or add try/except

mcqs.q: Which line of a traceback names the error type?
mcqs.why: A traceback ends with a line like ValueError: ..., naming the error and its message.

mcqs.q: Which error does int("abc") raise?
mcqs.why: "abc" is a string (right type) but not a valid number (wrong value), which is a ValueError.

mcqs.q: Which error means you used a variable that was never defined?
mcqs.why: Referring to an undefined name raises NameError.

mcqs.q: When does the else block of try / except / else run?
mcqs.why: else runs after a successful try; if an exception occurs, the matching except runs instead.

mcqs.q: When does the finally block run?
options: Always, whether or not an error occurred
mcqs.why: finally always executes, which makes it the right place for cleanup such as closing files.

lessons.title: Mini Project: Build a Quiz Game
lessons.body:
Mini Project: Build a Quiz Game

Time to build something complete. A quiz game needs three parts: data (a list of question dictionaries with a question, options and the correct answer), logic (a loop that asks each question, checks the answer and updates the score), and output (the final score and a message).

Store each question as a dictionary so the loop can treat every question the same way. Compare answers with .lower().strip() so "Paris", "paris" and " paris " all count as correct — small details like this are what make a program feel polished.

questions = [
    {"q": "What is the capital of France?", "a": "paris"},
    {"q": "What is 2 + 2?", "a": "4"},
]

score = 0
for item in questions:
    answer = input(item["q"] + " ").lower().strip()
    if answer == item["a"]:
        print("Correct!")
        score += 1
    else:
        print("The answer was", item["a"])

print("Your score:", score, "out of", len(questions))

The loop asks each question, normalises the answer, and adds 1 to the score when it matches. At the end it reports the score out of the number of questions. Extend it with more questions, a timer, or a play-again loop.

Key points

  • A list of dictionaries is a clean way to store quiz questions.
  • Loop over the questions so each one is handled the same way.
  • Use .lower().strip() so answers match regardless of case or spaces.
  • Keep a score variable and add 1 for each correct answer.
  • Report the final score out of the total number of questions.

mcqs.q: What is the best data structure for storing quiz questions with their answers?
mcqs.why: Each question is a dict with q and a keys, and the list keeps them in order for the loop.

mcqs.q: Why use .lower() on the player's answer?
options: To convert it to a number
So "Paris" and "paris" both count as correct
mcqs.why: lower() makes the comparison case-insensitive, so capitalisation does not mark a right answer wrong.

mcqs.q: How is the score updated for a correct answer?
mcqs.why: score += 1 adds one to the running total for each correct answer.

mcqs.q: What does input() return when the player types an answer?
mcqs.why: input() always returns text, which is why we compare it with the string answer.

mcqs.q: How do you know how many questions there are in total?
mcqs.why: len() counts the question dictionaries in the list, giving the total for the final score line.
